subjects.displayTitle: Divine love: the hidden treasure and the life of creation
subjects.introduction: What if love is more fundamental than the beings who experience it? These selections approach that question through the hidden treasure, the love that precedes creation, and the bonds that sustain human fellowship. Their language of God loving His own beauty belongs to a discussion of divine self-sufficiency and creative generosity; reading it through ordinary vanity would miss its purpose. At the same time, the insistence that the divine Essence exceeds all description places a limit on every image we employ. First John connects the unseen God, the sending of the Son, and the practice of loving one another [1]. That practical connection offers a fruitful companion to the metaphysical passages here. Read beside creation and the recognition of the Manifestations, these texts invite us to consider how an account of the origin of existence might change the quality of our relationships.
subjects.arc: Begin with love preceding human existence, explore its relation to divine transcendence and creation, and return to the love that binds a human family.

subjects.displayTitle: The stations of the Manifestation: one voice, several perspectives
subjects.introduction: A speaker may affirm complete servitude in one passage and speak with divine authority in another. How should we listen? These selections offer several ways of distinguishing the stations of a Manifestation: unity and distinction, humanity and divinity, or body, rational soul, and the manifestation of divine perfections. The different enumerations answer different questions, and need not be forced into one fixed diagram. The image of a mirror helps hold together the reality of the light and the distinction between its source and its place of appearance. Qur’an 18:110 brings human mortality, revelation, righteous action, and the oneness of God into a single utterance [1]. Read beside the knowledge of God and divine love, the compilation encourages attention to who is speaking, from which perspective, and toward what transformation in the hearer.
subjects.arc: Begin with divinity expressed through self-effacement, distinguish the principal perspectives, then consider how their voices appear in scripture and human experience.

subjects.displayTitle: The stages of creation: from possibility to fulfilment
subjects.introduction: Before a thing is made, there may be an inclination, a purpose, a measure, and a coming together of conditions. These selections use such distinctions to approach the mystery of creation, often through seven stages named Will, Purpose, predestination, fate, permission, fixed time, and the book. Their correspondences with letters, colours, elements, and human action invite patient comparison; differing translations and sequences should remain visible. Genesis offers another ordered account that culminates in a sanctified seventh day [1], while a selection here interprets its days as ranks of existence. That comparison opens inquiry without identifying the two schemes. Beside complementary principles and spiritual ascent, the subject asks how possibility becomes actuality, how necessary relationships coexist with action, and why a demanding metaphysical discussion might culminate in detachment rather than a claim to have exhausted the divine mystery.
subjects.arc: Establish the sevenfold vocabulary, explore its symbolic and practical explanations, compare distinct philosophical accounts, and return to responsibility and detachment.

subjects.displayTitle: Descent and ascent: the human being at the dawn
subjects.introduction: To stand at the lowest point of a circle can also mean standing where a new movement begins. These selections place the human being at that turning point: formed within the material world, yet capable of spiritual growth through education and the acquisition of virtues. Descent and ascent become images for bringing forth and creating anew, while the recurring language of motion challenges the idea of a finished or static creation. Ecclesiastes joins the return of dust to the earth with the return of spirit to God [1]; the compilation develops further accounts of return, progress, and the rejection of repeated earthly embodiment. Read beside creation’s stages and divine love, the circle invites a practical inquiry: what makes an upward movement visible in a life? The passages on education, cooperation, and reciprocity suggest that ascent concerns our relationships as well as our inward experience.
subjects.arc: Begin at the human turning point, trace the movement of creation and return, then explore spiritual progress through education and reciprocal service.

subjects.displayTitle: Creation in pairs: relationship, difference, and the creative word
subjects.introduction: A word and its meaning, an influence and its reception, two mirrors meeting: the images here suggest that relationship belongs to the very texture of created existence. The letters of the command to be become a way to explore how multiplicity arises, while passages on marriage, divine names, and complementary principles extend the theme in different directions. Qur’an 36:36 includes pairs among what the earth produces, among human beings, and beyond human knowledge [1]. Yet a selection here explicitly places spirit beyond masculine and feminine bodily characteristics. That distinction matters when interpreting parental or gendered metaphors. Beside the stages of creation and divine love, this compilation invites us to distinguish symbolic insight from a literal diagram of every reality, and to ask how difference can participate in unity without turning complementarity into a fixed hierarchy of human worth.
subjects.arc: Begin with the creative command, explore word and meaning and complementary realities, then test the reach and limits of the metaphors through spirit, relationship, and humility.

subjects.displayTitle: Knowing God: the unseen and the encounter with revelation
subjects.introduction: How can the unknowable become the object of a living relationship? These selections hold together the transcendence of the divine Essence and the recognition of the Manifestations, whose lives and words make divine attributes accessible. A mirror does not contain the sun, yet it can reveal its light: the image redirects knowledge from possession of an essence toward encounter with its signs. John’s account of Philip asking to see the Father offers a companion inquiry into seeing, knowing, words, and works [1]. The collection also asks readers to examine a claim with their own eyes, warns against substituting familiar names for recognition, and preserves a reminder of the infinity of divine mercy. Read beside the stations of the Manifestation and divine love, it invites both intellectual humility and a searching, responsible response to revelation.
subjects.arc: Begin with the visible and unseen, explore the mirror and the limits of conception, then move toward independent recognition, interpretation, and the scope of mercy.
